title: Why Japanese Schools Don't Employ Janitors to Clean Classrooms
hook: Japanese schools skip janitors not because tradition demands it, but because a postwar budget cut got dressed up decades later as moral education.
target_query: why do japanese schools not have janitors
free_section_html:
Japanese public schools do not employ janitors to clean classrooms because the daily cleaning routine, called souji (cleaning time), is built into the curriculum itself, with students doing the work in place of custodial staff. Most elementary and junior high schools set aside fifteen to twenty minutes after lunch, several days a week, during which classes split into small groups called han and rotate through assigned zones: classroom floors, hallways, stairwells, the gymnasium, sometimes the toilets. A rotating duty roster, touban, tracks who does what and when.

This is not an informal custom that schools happen to keep. It is written into the education ministry's curriculum guidelines, the gakushu shido yoryo, under a category called tokubetsu katsudo, or special activities, alongside student council work and club activities. Because it counts as instructional time rather than unpaid labor, schools are not required to hire outside cleaning staff for routine daily upkeep, and most don't.

Schools are not entirely staff-free, however. Larger facility maintenance, boiler repairs, grounds upkeep, and heavier custodial tasks are usually handled by a small number of technical or maintenance staff, sometimes called yomu-in, employed by the local board of education. What is absent is the daily janitor who mops floors and empties bins after students go home, a role many countries treat as a basic school expense.

The financial logic behind this setup is older than the moral framing usually attached to it. Occupation-era and early postwar Japan operated under severe budget constraints, and school custodial positions were among the line items that did not survive. What happened next is the more interesting part: an economic gap was gradually filled with an educational justification, one that now gets exported to schools abroad as if it had always been the point.
paid_body_html:
A Budget Decision Looking for a Rationale

In the years immediately after 1945, Japan's Ministry of Education was rebuilding a national school system on a fraction of its prewar resources. The School Education Law of 1947 restructured compulsory schooling but said nothing about who would sweep the floors. Local boards of education, strapped for cash, quietly stopped budgeting for janitorial staff in most elementary and junior high schools. Students had already been cleaning their own classrooms in some form since the Meiji era, when schools borrowed the ethic of household chores as part of character training, but the postwar period is when the practice became close to universal by necessity rather than choice.

For roughly two decades, souji operated as an unglamorous administrative fact rather than a celebrated pedagogy. It saved money. It kept custodial costs off already thin municipal budgets. Nobody in the ministry was writing essays about the character-building power of a mop.

How Souji Became Moral Education

The philosophical packaging came later, and it borrowed heavily from Zen Buddhist monastic practice, specifically samu, the manual labor monks perform as a form of meditation and discipline rather than as chores to be delegated. Education officials and teachers, looking to justify a cost-saving arrangement that had become entrenched, found in samu a ready-made vocabulary: cleaning as training in attentiveness, humility, and care for shared space, not as a task beneath a student's dignity.

This reframing shows up explicitly in later revisions of the curriculum guidelines, where cleaning time is grouped with student government and ceremonial activities under tokubetsu katsudo. The shift matters because it changed souji's legal and cultural status. What began as an absence of paid staff became an affirmative claim about what children should learn. Teachers began describing the fifteen minutes after lunch not as work students do because no one else will, but as training in noticing dirt, taking responsibility for shared property, and functioning as part of a group, values that align closely with broader goals of Japanese compulsory education around collective responsibility.

The Export Problem

Souji has become one of Japan's most imitated classroom practices abroad, adopted in modified form by a number of international schools and by some charter school networks in the United States that emphasize discipline and collective responsibility. The imported versions tend to borrow the ritual, students wiping down desks, straightening chairs, without importing the institutional scaffolding that makes it function in Japan: a fixed daily slot inside the official curriculum, a rotation system with clear roles, dedicated cleaning tools stored in every classroom, and a staff culture where homeroom teachers participate alongside students rather than supervising from a distance.

Critics of these transplants argue the practice can curdle into something closer to unpaid labor extraction when it is added on top of an already packed school day rather than built into the timetable, or when it is applied selectively as a disciplinary tool rather than a universal routine. In Japan, souji applies to every student, every day, regardless of academic performance or behavior, which is part of why it reads as education rather than punishment. Strip that universality out and the same fifteen minutes can look very different.

Where the System Is Actually Under Strain

Inside Japan, souji faces quieter pressures that rarely make it into admiring foreign coverage. Teacher workload reform, driven by growing concern over unpaid overtime among Japanese teachers, has pushed some schools to question whether staff should be supervising cleaning at all rather than using that time for lesson preparation. A small but growing number of schools, particularly in urban areas with tighter facility budgets, have begun outsourcing bathroom cleaning specifically, citing hygiene standards and the physical demands of that particular task on young children.

There is also a recurring, low-level debate among parents' associations, PTA groups, about chemical cleaning products, appropriate supervision during cleaning of stairwells and windows, and whether students in the earliest grades should be handling cleaning duties involving toilets at all. None of this has dislodged souji as a near-universal practice, but it has softened its edges: more schools now exempt the youngest students from certain tasks, and a handful have reduced daily souji to a few days a week rather than every day.

What the Practice Actually Reveals

The more useful way to read souji is not as evidence of some innate Japanese orderliness, but as a case study in how institutions retroactively moralize their own budget constraints. The cleaning happens because, decades ago, someone decided it was cheaper for students to do it. The meaning attached to that decision, discipline, humility, shared ownership of space, arrived afterward and has proven durable enough that even well-funded schools that could easily afford janitors choose not to hire them. That durability is the real story: a cost-saving measure that outlived its original justification because the replacement justification turned out to be more persuasive than the truth.
key_takeaways: Japanese schools skip janitors mainly because souji, daily student-led cleaning, is written into official curriculum guidelines as "special activities," not because of unbroken tradition alone.
The practice traces to postwar budget shortages after 1947, when local boards of education stopped funding custodial staff for daily cleaning in most schools.
Zen Buddhist samu (monastic manual labor) was invoked later to justify the arrangement philosophically, turning a cost-saving measure into a moral education narrative.
Schools still employ maintenance staff for major repairs and grounds work; what's absent is the daily janitor role common in many other countries.

Foreign schools that import souji as a ritual without its institutional scaffolding, dedicated time, universal application, shared teacher participation, risk turning it into unpaid labor rather than education.
